title: Queue Using Two Stacks
directAnswer: Keep two stacks: an inbox for pushes and an outbox for pops/peeks. enqueue always pushes onto inbox. dequeue/peek work on outbox; when outbox is empty, pour the entire inbox into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top. Each element moves at most once between stacks, giving amortized O(1) per operation even though a single dequeue can be O(n).

remember.pattern: Two stacks reverse each other → FIFO from LIFO
rules: Only refill the outbox when it is **empty** — refilling early scrambles the order.
Pour the **entire** inbox into the outbox in one go, not one element at a time.
Reversing a stack once (LIFO) and reading it gives FIFO — that single reversal is the whole trick.
dequeue is O(n) on the transfer step but **amortized O(1)**: each element is moved at most twice total (in, then out).
Never push directly onto the outbox in enqueue — that breaks the ordering invariant.
whenToUse: You only have stacks (LIFO) but need queue (FIFO) semantics
Building one ADT out of another in a design / OOP question
Amortized analysis is acceptable (no hard per-op latency cap)
Implementing iterative tree traversal or undo/redo with ordering flips
antiSignals: A native queue / deque is available → just use it, O(1) guaranteed
Hard real-time worst-case O(1) per op required → two stacks give amortized, not worst-case
You need random access or indexing → neither a stack nor a queue fits
remember.takeaway: Reversing a LIFO structure turns it into a FIFO one. Two stacks, with a lazy one-direction transfer, is the classic 'build one data structure from another' answer — and the amortized argument (each item moves a constant number of times) is the reusable idea.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that reversing a stack yields a queue, and whether you can justify amortized O(1) instead of claiming a single dequeue is O(1).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Transferring elements back and forth on every operation (O(n) each), or refilling the outbox while it still has elements, which corrupts the order.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the invariant ('outbox holds the front of the queue, oldest on top'), refill only when outbox is empty, and give the amortized argument: each element is pushed and popped at most twice.

problemStatement:
Implement a first-in-first-out (FIFO) **queue** using only two **stacks**. The implemented queue must support all the standard operations:

- `enqueue(x)` — add element `x` to the back of the queue.
- `dequeue()` — remove and return the element at the front of the queue.
- `peek()` — return the element at the front without removing it.
- `empty()` — return whether the queue is empty.

You may only use the standard stack operations: push to top, pop from top, peek at top, size, and is-empty.
constraints: At most 10⁵ calls total across enqueue, dequeue, peek, empty
dequeue and peek are only called on a non-empty queue
Only stack operations may be used internally — no native queue/deque
understanding: A stack returns the most recently added element (LIFO); a queue must return the least recently added (FIFO). One reversal converts one into the other, so the design hinges on reversing elements exactly once and reusing that reversed order until it runs out.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are dequeue and peek ever called on an empty queue?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per the constraints, no. If they could be, decide whether to return a sentinel or throw — say it out loud.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is amortized O(1) acceptable, or do you need worst-case O(1) per operation?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Two stacks give amortized O(1). True worst-case O(1) needs a more complex design (e.g. three stacks with incremental copying).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use the language's built-in stack type?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — ArrayDeque in Java or a list in Python, used strictly as a stack. You just can't use a native queue.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should peek and dequeue share the refill logic?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — both need the front element, so both trigger a refill when the outbox is empty. Factor it into one helper.

examples.explanation: 1 was enqueued first, so it's the front. peek returns 1 without removing; dequeue removes and returns 1; 2 still remains so empty is false.
First dequeue pours [1,2,3] from inbox into outbox as [3,2,1] (1 on top), returns 1. Second dequeue reuses outbox, returns 2 — no refill needed.
Refill happens twice because the outbox empties between dequeues — but each element still moves at most twice overall.

approaches.name: Costly Dequeue — Reverse on Every Removal
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it as the obvious first design, then point out the per-dequeue O(n) cost and improve it with lazy transfer.
hints: enqueue is easy — push onto a stack. The hard part is that the element you want to remove is at the BOTTOM of that stack. How do you reach the bottom of a stack?
To remove the front, pour everything into a second stack so the bottom element rises to the top, pop it, then pour everything back.
This works but every dequeue moves all n elements twice. Can you avoid pouring back?
approaches.complexityReasoning: enqueue is a single push, O(1). dequeue moves all n elements to the second stack and back, so each removal is O(n); n removals cost O(n²) in total.
approaches.explanation:
The naive design makes `enqueue` cheap and `dequeue` expensive. Push every element onto the inbox stack. To dequeue, the front of the queue is the element at the *bottom* of the inbox — unreachable directly. So pour the whole inbox into a temporary stack (reversing it, front now on top), pop the front, then pour everything back into the inbox.

**Why pour back.** In this design the inbox is the single source of truth, always holding elements newest-on-top. After grabbing the front you restore that invariant by returning every remaining element to the inbox, ready for the next enqueue.

**Why this is correct but slow.** Each dequeue touches all n elements twice — once out, once back — so a single dequeue is O(n) and a sequence of n dequeues is O(n²). For 10⁵ operations that's up to 10¹⁰ moves. Correct, easy to reason about, but quadratic.

**The wasteful part.** Notice we pour everything back only to pour it out again on the very next dequeue. That round trip is pure waste. The optimal version simply *leaves* the reversed elements in the outbox and reuses them until they run out — turning repeated O(n) work into amortized O(1).
approaches.insight: The reversal idea is already correct here; the inefficiency is restoring the inbox after every dequeue. Recognising that the reversed order can be kept and reused is the leap to the optimal solution.

dryRun.intro: Everything lives in the inbox; dequeue pours out, pops the front, then pours back.

java.explanation: enqueue is a single push — newest element on top.
Pour the whole inbox into temp, reversing it so the queue front rises to the top.
The oldest element is now on top of temp — that's the queue front.
Restore everything to the inbox — this pour-back is the O(n) waste the optimal version removes.

Drain the inbox into temp, reversing order.
Top of temp is the oldest element — the front.
Pour back to restore the inbox; repeated every dequeue, hence O(n) each.

pitfalls: Pouring back after every dequeue — pure wasted work, O(n) per call.
Forgetting to restore the inbox, which loses the FIFO ordering on the next enqueue.

approaches.name: Two Stacks — Lazy Transfer (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'refill the outbox only when it's empty' and give the amortized O(1) argument.
hints: What if you didn't pour everything back after a dequeue? Could you leave the reversed elements somewhere and keep popping them?
Use two stacks: inbox for enqueue, outbox for dequeue/peek. Only when the outbox is empty do you pour the entire inbox into it.
Each element is pushed onto inbox once, then moved to outbox once, then popped once — at most a constant number of touches. That's why it's amortized O(1) despite the occasional O(n) refill.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Any element is pushed to inbox, moved to outbox, and popped exactly once over its lifetime — 3 constant-cost touches. Across m operations the total work is O(m), so each operation is amortized O(1). enqueue is always O(1); a dequeue that triggers a refill is O(n) but pays for the many cheap dequeues that follow.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain two stacks with distinct jobs. The **inbox** receives every `enqueue` (O(1) push). The **outbox** serves every `dequeue` and `peek`. The key rule: only when the outbox is empty do you pour the *entire* inbox into it. Pouring one stack into another reverses it, so the oldest element — the true queue front — ends up on top of the outbox.

**The invariant that makes it correct.** At all times the outbox holds a *prefix of the queue front* with the oldest element on top, and the inbox holds the *more recent* elements newest on top. Reading the queue front means: if the outbox has anything, its top is the front; otherwise refill from the inbox first. Because we only refill an *empty* outbox, we never interleave a fresh batch on top of an older one — that would scramble the order. This is the single most important rule.

**Why the reversal gives FIFO.** Suppose you enqueue 1, 2, 3. The inbox is [1, 2, 3] with 3 on top. Pour it into the outbox one pop at a time: pop 3, push 3; pop 2, push 2; pop 1, push 1. The outbox is now [3, 2, 1] with **1 on top**. Popping the outbox yields 1, 2, 3 — exactly FIFO. One reversal flips LIFO into FIFO.

**Why this is amortized O(1), not O(1).** A dequeue that finds an empty outbox does O(n) work to refill. But every element participates in a refill *at most once* — once it's in the outbox it's never moved again, only popped. So over a run of operations the expensive refills are rare and each element's total cost is constant: one inbox push, one move, one outbox pop. Dividing total work by the number of operations gives O(1) *amortized*. Be precise in an interview: say 'amortized', and if asked for worst-case-per-op O(1), note that needs a more elaborate design.

**Why peek shares the refill.** `peek` also needs the front, so it runs the same 'refill if empty' step and then reads (not pops) the outbox top. Factor the refill into a private helper both methods call.
approaches.insight: The whole speedup comes from *not undoing work*. The costly version reverses and then un-reverses on every dequeue; the lazy version reverses once and reuses that order until exhausted. 'Do the expensive transformation once and reuse it' is the reusable amortization idea — the same reasoning behind dynamic-array doubling and splay-tree restructuring.

edgeCases.behavior: First dequeue refills outbox with [1], pops 1. enqueue(2) goes to inbox. peek finds outbox empty, refills with [2], returns 2 without removing.
Refills happen whenever the outbox drains, but each element is still moved at most twice overall — amortization holds.

edgeCases.input: empty() with elements split across stacks
edgeCases.behavior: Returns false unless BOTH inbox and outbox are empty; checking only one stack is a bug.

pitfalls: Refilling the outbox when it is NOT empty — interleaves new and old batches and breaks FIFO order.
Checking only one stack in empty() — elements can sit in either.
Claiming worst-case O(1) per dequeue — it's amortized; a refill is O(n).

commonMistakes: Pouring elements back to the inbox after every dequeue, making each removal O(n).
Refilling the outbox while it still has elements, scrambling the order.
Implementing empty() by checking only one of the two stacks.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Refilling a non-empty outbox
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you pour the inbox in while the outbox still has older elements, the newer batch lands on top and gets served before the older one — FIFO is violated.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: empty() checks only one stack
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After a refill, elements live in the outbox while the inbox is empty (and vice versa). Testing a single stack reports the queue empty when it isn't.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def empty(self) -> bool:
    return not self.inbox
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
def empty(self) -> bool:
    return not self.inbox and not self.outbox

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pouring back every dequeue
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Restoring the inbox after each removal throws away the reversed order you just built, forcing an O(n) reversal on the very next dequeue.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
front = temp.pop()
while temp:
    self.inbox.append(temp.pop())  # wasteful restore
return front
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
self._shift_if_needed()
return self.outbox.pop()  # reuse the reversed outbox until empty
